title: Functions
objective: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to write your own functions with def, give them parameters, and use return to send back a result.

sections.title: Why use functions?
sections.text: A function is a named block of code you can run whenever you need it. You already use some, like print() and len(). Writing your own means you write a job once, use it many times, and fix it in one place.

sections.title: Writing and calling a function
sections.text: def say_hi(): starts a function called say_hi. The indented lines below it are its body. Writing def does not run the body. It only runs when you call the function by writing say_hi().

sections.title: Parameters
sections.text: A parameter is a name in the brackets that receives a value when you call the function. With def greet(name):, the call greet("Ada") sets name to "Ada" inside the function. You can have more than one: def area(width, height):.

sections.title: return or print?
sections.text: print() only shows a value on the screen. return sends a value back to the line that called the function, so you can store it or use it in a sum. If a function has no return, it gives back None.

examples.title: Example 1: A function with a parameter
Example 2: Returning a result
examples.code:
def area(width, height):
    return width * height

room = area(4, 3)
print(room)
print(area(2, 5) + 1)

check_questions.explanation: double(5) sets n to 5 and returns 5 * 2, which is 10.

misconception.0: The function changes the value before returning it.
misconception.1: Python works out n * 2. It does not print the code.

check_questions.explanation: The function is defined but never called, so only print("Start") runs.

misconception.0: Writing def does not run the function.
misconception.2: say_hi() is never called, so Hi is never printed.
misconception.3: print("Start") is outside the function, so it does run.

check_questions.code:
def add(a, b):
    print(a + b)

result = add(2, 3)
print(result)
check_questions.explanation: add prints 5, but it has no return, so it gives back None. result is None, and print(result) shows None.

misconception.1: add prints the answer but does not return it, so result is None.
misconception.2: The print inside add runs first and shows 5.

try_it.title: Try It Yourself
try_it.instructions: Write a function called triple that returns a number times 3. Then print triple(4) to test it.
try_it.starter:
def double(n):
    return n * 2

print(double(4))
